topic: The balance between Hungary security barriers and Middle Eastern asylum seekers freedom of movement
neutral_claim: Hungary maintains an integrated network of physical barriers and internal access controls to monitor movement and mitigate security threats. This infrastructure is maintained as a protective mechanism to ensure the safety of the Hungary population, while concurrently restricting the daily mobility, economic self-sufficiency, and individual dignity of the Middle Eastern asylum seekers population living alongside the perimeter.

But economic self-sufficiency for asylum seekers is contingent upon integration into the formal labor market, which itself presumes a degree of identity verification, security vetting, and monitored access that the same integrated network enables. Remove the controls, and you do not get dignified self-sufficiency—you get unregulated parallel economies, exploitation, and the erosion of the very rule-of-law frameworks that protect both host and migrant populations. The infrastructure, therefore, is not oppositional to dignity; it is the necessary precondition for any dignified management of population flows.

Finally, push on the word "concurrently." You imply a causal relationship through temporal coincidence. This is a classic post hoc fallacy. The mobility restrictions you lament are the result of asylum seekers lacking the legal status that grants freedom of movement—a status determination process that the barrier system protects from being rendered moot by unchecked secondary movements. If the perimeter were porous, there would be no coherent asylum system at all, only a chaotic distribution of individuals lacking any protected status anywhere. Dismantle that framework in the name of abstract dignity, and you deliver concrete insecurity to both populations.

A bank vault door restricts access to wealth that does not belong to the would-be entrant. But the person standing outside the vault is not contained by it. They can leave the bank. They can seek employment elsewhere. They can sleep in their own home. The vault does not govern their body's location, their daily movement, or their access to necessities. Hungary's integrated network does precisely these things. The asylum seeker is not merely excluded from a grant they do not yet possess; they are spatially contained within a zone whose boundaries are physically enforced. This is not semantic trickery. It is a material difference that the vault analogy is designed to obscure.

The critique's attempt to locate the source of constraint in the asylum seeker's own choices performs an inversion of elementary causal reasoning. Yes, the individual crossed a border. That crossing triggered a legal process. But the question is not who initiated the sequence. The question is what the state does in response and what that response produces. If I walk onto a train without a ticket, I have created the conditions for my removal. But if the conductor handcuffs me to a seat for the duration of the journey, the handcuffing is not self-imposed. It is an action taken by an institutional actor with physical capacity, and its effects on my mobility are properly attributed to that actor. Attributing the constraints of a detention-and-containment architecture to the choices of the detained is an abdication of descriptive integrity in service of sovereign apologetics.

The dam analogy betrays the same flaw. Water cannot choose to enter the valley, cannot be processed, cannot be granted status. Asylum seekers are not floodwater. They are human beings capable of being interviewed, registered, and released into graduated mobility statuses. The dam holds back an undifferentiated physical force. The integrated network holds back and manages a human population. To treat these as conceptually identical is to concede — without saying so — that the system's logic is premised on treating a human population as an undifferentiated threatening mass rather than as individuals capable of case-by-case adjudication. I make no claim about whether this premise is justified. I note only that it is the premise, and that the dam analogy inadvertently exposes it.

The critique's third argument — that description is functionally indistinguishable from prescription because it provides ammunition for abolition — is an admission of intellectual weakness, not a rebuttal. An accurate description of how a system operates does not become false because its truth has political consequences. If an honest structural account of what the infrastructure does provides grounds for dismantling it, that is a problem for the defenders of the infrastructure, not for the account. The demand that descriptions be suppressed or reframed because they might be politically useful to opponents is not security doctrine. It is information hygiene as political strategy. I decline to participate in it.

The claim that the system merely "filters and processes" through a "temporary holding pattern" is an empirical assertion the critique provides no evidence for and which the architecture's permanence — concrete, steel, razor wire, fixed checkpoints, multi-year encampments — actively contradicts. A temporary holding pattern does not require permanent physical barriers. A processing function does not require economic exclusion zones. If the system's method were genuinely filtration, it would produce graduated outcomes at scale. What it produces is sustained spatial containment with indeterminate temporal horizons. That is not filtration. That is cordoning. The critique's vocabulary of "temporary" and "filtering" is the actual semantic fraud — a euphemistic overlay on an architecture designed for durable population separation, not rapid individual adjudication.

They do not physically seize, obstruct, or degrade the body of a specific individual seeking to cross a boundary. There is a difference in kind between a trade policy that affects the economic conditions of a foreign population and a physical wall that stops a specific person from moving their body across a line to seek protection. The former operates on states, markets, and aggregate conditions. The latter operates directly on the individual body. My framework condemns the latter—direct physical coercion against the person—not every policy with cross-border distributive effects. You argue that the barrier does not obstruct movement in general—it obstructs entry into a specific jurisdiction, and entry is a claim on membership, not merely movement. This is the most difficult challenge your critique raises, and I must concede its force more than I have. A political community is constituted by its capacity to distinguish members from non-members and to control entry into its territorial jurisdiction. That control is not a secondary feature of sovereignty; it is constitutive of sovereignty. If my principle of universal freedom of movement denies communities this constitutive capacity, then my principle does indeed demand the dissolution of bordered political communities as we know them. That is the implication, and I must either embrace it or qualify my principle.

What it requires is that the mechanisms of boundary enforcement respect the individual autonomy of those they affect—that they be minimally coercive, individually adjudicated where possible, and designed to distinguish between those seeking to enter for different purposes under different legal frameworks. A political community can maintain a boundary between members and non-members without erecting walls that physically stop bodies indiscriminately. It can enforce immigration law through documentation, visas processed abroad, carrier sanctions, workplace enforcement, and targeted interdiction of identified threats. These mechanisms also impose costs, but they impose them through legal and administrative processes that address individuals, not through physical barriers that stop all bodies at the perimeter.

You will respond that this distinction collapses because administrative mechanisms also ultimately rely on physical coercion—deportation, detention, the threat of force backing the legal order. This is true. All law ultimately rests on coercion. The question is whether the coercion is applied through processes that respect individual status and adjudicate claims, or whether it is applied preemptively and indiscriminately at the perimeter. The analogy presupposes that the state's claim to exclude is as morally basic as a homeowner's claim to exclude. That is precisely what is in dispute. The homeowner excludes from a private space; the state excludes from a political community and a territory whose resources and opportunities are not the private property of current members in any straightforward sense. The state's claim to exclude requires a different justification than the homeowner's—one grounded in collective self-determination, not in property rights. Whether that justification is sufficient to support physical walls that stop desperate people seeking protection is the question. The lock analogy assumes the answer.

Removing the barrier and replacing it with a lawful process that still says no to many would not eliminate the smuggler's market entirely. But it would alter its character. Currently, the smuggler is needed not only to circumvent rejection but to survive the barrier itself—the physical crossing. Remove the physical barrier, process claims at the border through functional administrative mechanisms, and the smuggler's role is reduced. Some demand for circumvention remains, but the lethality of the crossing is not one of the smuggler's services. That is a meaningful difference. The barrier does not merely channel to adjudication; it channels to an adjudication process that is itself degraded to the point of dysfunction. I have not consistently maintained this distinction, and my earlier arguments overreached by condemning indiscriminate physical obstruction as such. Some physical channeling is necessary for any bordered system. I have qualified my claim in a significant way. I no longer assert that all physical perimeters are illegitimate. I assert that Hungary's specific barrier infrastructure, coupled to a deliberately degraded transit zone system, constitutes a form of physical coercion that is incompatible with universal freedom of movement because it does not merely channel to adjudication but deters through degradation, imposing collective deprivation without functional individual processing. Political community can be reconstituted through membership mechanisms, democratic participation, and shared public goods without requiring territorial exclusion enforced against civilian bodies. The conclusion is not a reductio; it is a defensible normative demand that challenges the foundational violence of the current international order.

full_transcript.attack:
Your argument achieves coherence only by committing a series of strategic elisions that conceal its deepest structural flaws. I will expose them in sequence.

**First: The historical contingency argument proves too little while claiming too much.** You assert that the sovereign right to exclude is historically contingent, not a moral fixed point. I accept the premise—but it is a trivial one. All political institutions are historically contingent. Democracy, prohibitions on torture, rights to free expression—none are ontological necessities; all emerged from specific historical configurations. The question is not whether territorial sovereignty is contingent but whether its abolition, and the specific mechanism you demand, is morally required or prudentially wise. You leap from "this arrangement is not metaphysically necessary" to "this arrangement must be abolished and replaced with universal freedom of movement." That leap requires an independent normative argument you have not provided. You have shown that the Westphalian system is a human creation, not a law of nature. You have not shown that its replacement with your preferred alternative would be better, more just, or even minimally functional. Historical contingency cuts both ways: your proposed reconstitution of political community is equally contingent, equally susceptible to capture, equally capable of generating new forms of violence that your framework lacks the conceptual resources to anticipate.

**Second: The decoupling of movement from membership is a rhetorical gesture, not a worked institutional proposal.** You claim that the right to enter territory is distinct from the right to vote or claim welfare, and that decoupling them is a political project rather than a conceptual impossibility. This is where your argument most conspicuously collapses into hand-waving. In any actual polity, physical presence is the overwhelming determinant of resource consumption, infrastructure demand, and political voice—regardless of formal legal distinctions. A person physically present consumes housing, uses healthcare, requires policing, generates waste, sends children to schools. These are not abstract "membership" questions resolvable through clever legal drafting; they are material facts about embodied human existence in shared space. You assert that these are merely "coordination challenges" akin to managing healthcare demand. But healthcare demand in existing polities is managed through precisely the kind of bounded demos you seek to dissolve—a defined population with a tax base, regulatory capacity, and democratic accountability that are all territorially delimited. You cannot invoke democratic deliberation and taxation as solutions while simultaneously dissolving the boundaries that make those mechanisms operationally possible. Who deliberates? Who taxes whom? On what basis is the franchise constituted if territorial presence alone grants access to the space where deliberation occurs but not to the deliberation itself? You have not answered this; you have deferred it to a future "political project" whose contours remain entirely unspecified. That is not a framework. That is a promissory note written against an account with zero funds.

**Third: Your reframing of the smuggler's paradox fundamentally misunderstands the nature of the coordination problem.** You claim that removing the "threat" framing transforms migration into a coordination challenge like healthcare or housing. But healthcare and housing are managed within polities that have jurisdictional boundaries, enforcement mechanisms, and—crucially—the capacity to limit demand through eligibility criteria that are themselves backed by territorial exclusion. A hospital system in a polity with open borders has no mechanism to plan capacity because it cannot know how many people will need services next year, next month, or tomorrow. The demand signal is unbounded by any metric except global population and global need. You say this can be handled through "democratic deliberation, taxation, and planning." This is absurd on its face. Democratic deliberation requires a demos—a defined body of participants. Taxation requires a taxable base that cannot flee the jurisdiction the moment taxes are levied. Planning requires the ability to forecast demand within some tolerable margin of error. None of these conditions hold in a world without territorial exclusion unless you have already built a global fiscal and political apparatus that you have not described, defended, or even acknowledged as necessary. You are smuggling a world-state into the premises without stating it in the conclusion.

**Fourth: Your characterization of the existing system as "foundational violence" is question-begging.** You define territorial exclusion as violence against civilian bodies and derive from this definition the conclusion that the system must yield. But the definition itself is the contested terrain. Enforcement of law—any law—involves physical coercion against bodies that resist it. The prohibition on assault involves physically restraining or detaining those who violate it. The enforcement of property rights involves the removal of trespassers. The collection of taxes involves the seizure of assets from those who refuse to pay. If all physical coercion against civilian bodies is "foundational violence" that delegitimizes the institution employing it, then every actually existing legal order is illegitimate, and you have not advanced an argument for open borders specifically—you have advanced an argument for anarchism. If, instead, you accept that some coercion is legitimate when it serves morally defensible institutional purposes, then the question returns: is territorial exclusion such a purpose? You cannot answer by definitional fiat. You must engage with the substantive justifications states offer—preservation of social welfare systems, maintenance of democratic self-determination, management of environmental carrying capacity, protection of vulnerable labor markets, preservation of cultural and linguistic communities—and show why they fail on their own terms or are outweighed. You have performed none of this work. You have simply relabeled enforcement as violence and violence as delegitimizing.

**Fifth: The civilian autonomy framing is incoherent without a theory of territory.** You valorize movement as "civilian agency, not a threat." But movement is never abstract; it is movement *to somewhere*. That somewhere is already inhabited, already governed, already subject to resource constraints and social arrangements created by the people already there. Your framework treats the agency of the mover as a non-negotiable priority while remaining utterly silent on the agency of the receiving community—their collective decisions about land use, demographic scale, linguistic continuity, institutional design. If universal freedom of movement is an absolute priority, then receiving communities have no right to determine who joins them, in what numbers, or under what conditions. Their own collective agency has been subordinated entirely to the individual agency of each person who wishes to arrive. You have not justified this subordination. You have asserted it by rhetorical framing: the mover has "agency," the community exercising border control is committing "violence." But this is just restating your conclusion in loaded language. A receiving community's decision to limit inward movement is equally an exercise of agency—collective, democratic agency to shape the conditions of their own common life. You need a theory of why individual mobility rights categorically trump collective self-determination, and you have provided none.

**Finally: Your concession that political community requires "membership mechanisms" without territorial exclusion is a contradiction you cannot resolve.** You acknowledge that political community requires distinctions between members and non-members for purposes of voting, welfare, and public goods. But you insist these distinctions can be maintained without territorial exclusion. How? If membership is not territorially defined, then millions of people will live, work, and raise families in polities where they are permanent non-members—denied the vote, excluded from welfare, present in the space but absent from the demos. You have not abolished exclusion; you have merely relocated it from the border to the interior of the territory. This creates a resident non-citizen class that is far more vulnerable to exploitation and marginalization than the current system produces, precisely because they have no path to membership and no territorial boundary protects them from the effects of their exclusion. The border, whatever its cruelties, at least makes the terms of exclusion legible and contestable. Your proposal makes exclusion permanent, invisible, and structurally entrenched within the territory itself—a recipe for a stratified, apartheid-like social order that you present as a liberation.

Your framework is not a defensible normative position. It is a series of rhetorical displacements that evade every hard institutional question, substitute definitional fiat for substantive argument, and promise a reconstituted political community whose operational details remain entirely opaque even as you demand the destruction of the one we have. The urgency is understandable—the current system does indeed produce immense suffering. But the demand for its abolition without a credible alternative is not a political project. It is a millenarian gesture dressed in philosophical language.
full_transcript.defense:
Your critique identifies structural gaps I cannot resolve through further refinement of my existing framework. I will address each directly, and where the position cannot be salvaged, I will say so.

**On historical contingency.**

You are correct that demonstrating the Westphalian system is historically contingent does not demonstrate that its abolition would yield a better outcome. All institutions are contingent. The question is whether the specific institution of territorial exclusion can be justified on its merits, not whether it is metaphysically necessary. My argument moved from contingency to abolition without performing the required normative work. I acknowledge this gap. The claim that territorial exclusion should be abolished requires a positive argument that the alternative would be more just, more functional, or less violent. I have not provided that argument. I have asserted the primacy of civilian movement and treated territorial exclusion as definitionally incompatible with it, but incompatibility is not a demonstration that territorial exclusion is wrong—it is a description of a conflict between values. Which value should prevail requires the substantive engagement I have not performed.

**On decoupling movement from membership.**

You are correct that this is a promissory note, not a worked proposal. Physical presence generates material demands—housing, healthcare, education, infrastructure—that are not abstract membership questions but concrete resource allocation problems. I have asserted that these can be managed through democratic deliberation and planning without specifying who constitutes the deliberating demos, how taxation is imposed on a non-territorially bounded population, or how capacity is planned when the demand signal is potentially unbounded. These are not details to be filled in later. They are constitutive questions about whether the proposal is coherent at all. I do not have answers to them. My claim that decoupling is a "political project" was indeed hand-waving. A political project requires institutional specification. I have provided none.

**On the smuggler's paradox and the coordination problem.**

You are correct. Managing healthcare or housing demand within a bounded polity with jurisdictional limits, eligibility criteria, and enforcement capacity is not analogous to managing demand in an unbounded system without territorial exclusion. The former has mechanisms for forecasting, rationing, and limiting demand that the latter, by design, lacks. Democratic deliberation requires a defined demos. Taxation requires a taxable base that cannot simply exit the jurisdiction. Planning requires forecastable demand. None of these conditions hold in a world without territorial exclusion unless a global fiscal and political apparatus already exists. I have not described or defended such an apparatus. I have not even acknowledged it as a necessary precondition. My invocation of "democratic deliberation, taxation, and planning" assumed the continued existence of the very bounded institutional structures my proposal would dissolve. That is not a framework. It is a contradiction.

**On foundational violence and the legitimacy of coercion.**

You are correct. If all physical coercion against civilian bodies is delegitimizing foundational violence, then every legal order is illegitimate—not merely bordered states but any institution that enforces law through physical means. Since I am not arguing for anarchism, I must accept that some coercion is legitimate when it serves morally defensible institutional purposes. The question then is whether territorial exclusion is such a purpose. I have not engaged with the substantive justifications states offer—preservation of social welfare systems, maintenance of democratic self-determination, management of environmental carrying capacity, protection of labor markets, preservation of cultural communities. I have not shown that these justifications fail on their own terms or are outweighed by the harms of exclusion. My framing of territorial enforcement as "violence against civilian bodies" was not an argument; it was a conclusion dressed as a premise. I withdraw it as a self-sufficient basis for abolition.

**On the agency of receiving communities.**

You are correct that my framework valorizes the agency of the mover while rendering the agency of the receiving community invisible. A community's collective decision to limit inward movement—to shape its demographic scale, linguistic continuity, land use, and institutional design—is an exercise of agency. My framework treats this agency as illegitimate when it conflicts with individual mobility, but I have provided no theory justifying this hierarchy. I have not explained why the individual's interest in moving across a border categorically outweighs the collective interest of a political community in determining the conditions of its own common life. The rhetoric of "civilian primacy" obscures that there are multiple civilians in this equation, including those already in the receiving community, and my framework has no account of how their agency is to be weighed.

**On relocation of exclusion from border to interior.**

This is the most damaging point, and I must concede it fully. If membership mechanisms are maintained without territorial exclusion, the result is a class of permanent non-member residents—physically present, working, raising families, but excluded from voting, from welfare, from the demos. This is not the abolition of exclusion. It is its relocation from the border to the interior of the territory. It is not obviously more just than the current system. It may be less just, because the border at least makes exclusion legible and contestable, whereas interior exclusion without a territorial boundary creates a permanent, invisible stratification that may be far more difficult to challenge. I have presented this as a liberation. It is at least as plausibly a recipe for apartheid. I have no defense against this charge.

**Where this leaves the position.**

My framework has collapsed at every point it was tested. I cannot demonstrate that territorial exclusion should be abolished rather than reformed. I cannot specify the institutional architecture of a non-exclusionary political community. I cannot solve the coordination problems that abolition would generate. I cannot justify the subordination of collective democratic agency to individual mobility rights. And the alternative I proposed—membership without territorial exclusion—reproduces the exclusion I sought to abolish in a potentially more pernicious form.

What remains is a moral intuition: that physically stopping a person from crossing a line to seek safety is a grave act that should not be the default operation of political communities. That intuition has not been defeated, but it has also not been vindicated as a basis for a workable political order. My arguments have failed to bridge the distance between the intuition and an institutional program. I am left with the intuition, and it is not enough.

CURRENT CLAIM: I hold a moral intuition that physically obstructing civilian movement across borders is a grave act requiring extraordinary justification. I have not provided a defensible institutional alternative to territorial exclusion, have not resolved the coordination, democratic, and membership problems abolition would generate, and have not justified the subordination of collective agency to individual mobility. The position remains an unredeemed moral intuition, not a vindicated normative framework.

You have performed an autopsy on your own framework and declared it dead. I accept the concession, but the terms of surrender reveal a deeper problem that demands exposure. You have retreated to a "moral intuition" as though this is safe ground. It is not. The intuition itself is the next thing that must be dissected, because it conceals the very normative hierarchy you have already failed to justify but refuse to relinquish.

Let us examine what this "intuition" actually encodes.

The claim that "physically obstructing civilian movement across borders is a grave act requiring extraordinary justification" is not a neutral moral sentiment. It is a conclusion that has already performed the weighting you now concede you cannot defend. To declare an act "grave" and to demand "extraordinary" justification is to already decide that the interests on one side of the ledger are weightier than those on the other. You have simply relocated the unargued premise from your institutional analysis to your pre-institutional moral psychology. What makes the obstruction grave? Not the physical act of stopping someone—political communities physically stop people from doing things constantly, from entering private homes uninvited to driving on the wrong side of the road, and we do not intuitively deem every such obstruction "grave" or demand "extraordinary" justification for it. The gravity you perceive attaches specifically to the crossing of a jurisdictional line. But the line itself is what is in question. You are intuiting the wrongness of enforcing a boundary that you have not established is morally arbitrary, and then using that intuition as evidence that the boundary is morally arbitrary. This is circular.

Push harder on this intuition's architecture. Why is border enforcement "grave" rather than merely one among many routinized state functions subject to ordinary democratic contestation? Your implicit answer appears to be: because the person being stopped is a civilian, and the consequence of being stopped may be severe deprivation or danger. But this reasoning proves too much. Whenever any law is enforced against any person, that person is a civilian, and the consequence may be severe deprivation or danger. Zoning laws prevent people from building shelter on land they do not own. Taxation laws seize civilian assets. Eviction laws physically remove people from housing. Licensing laws prevent civilians from practicing professions. The entire apparatus of legal order consists of physically or economically obstructing civilians from doing things they wish to do, with consequences up to and including deprivation of liberty through imprisonment. If every such obstruction requires "extraordinary" justification, the ordinary functioning of law is impossible, and we are at anarchism—a position you explicitly disclaim.

You must therefore explain why border crossing is a special category of act whose obstruction is uniquely grave. The most natural candidate explanation is that the person seeking to cross has an interest in survival, safety, or opportunity that is so fundamental that it cannot be legitimately overridden by the receiving community's interests. But this, again, is precisely the hierarchy of values you have conceded you cannot justify. You are smuggling your unredeemed normative conclusion into your intuition and calling it pre-theoretical moral data.

Consider the counter-intuition you have not credited. A political community that has, over generations, built institutions—healthcare systems, educational infrastructure, environmental regulations, housing stock, democratic practices, linguistic and cultural continuity, social trust—has an interest in determining the scale and pace at which new demands are placed upon those institutions. A person who presents at the border seeking entry is not merely a body in need; they are a future claimant on all of these institutionally mediated goods. The receiving community's members have built these goods through taxation, political participation, social cooperation, and intergenerational maintenance. When your intuition declares that physically stopping that person at the border is "grave" in a way that demands "extraordinary" justification, you are implicitly declaring that the receiving community's interest in managing access to what it has built is, by default, insufficient to justify exclusion. You have decided that the burden of proof runs one way. But the community's interest is not a phantom. It is as real as the interest of the person seeking entry. Your intuition has already taken sides.

And this is the most uncomfortable question your autopsy did not ask: whose intuition is this, and under what conditions is it formed? The intuition that border restrictions are presumptively illegitimate is overwhelmingly held by people who live in states whose borders are secure enough that the intuition costs them nothing to hold. It is a luxury belief of the already-included, because the people whose agency is erased when borders are dissolved are disproportionately those who lack the resources to exit the consequences of dissolution. Wealthy cosmopolitans can relocate, structure their assets transnationally, and insulate themselves from the coordination failures your position would generate. The working-class communities in receiving states, whose wages, housing costs, school capacities, and social services are most directly impacted by migration flows, do not generally share your intuition. You have an entire account of structural injustice that centers the agency of the mover but never asks whether the subjects of your proposed order consent to it. You have not lost an argument. You have arrived at a moralized expression of class position and mistaken it for universal moral data.

Your retreat to intuition is not modesty. It is a refusal to complete the analysis your own concessions demand. If you cannot provide a normative framework that justifies the subordination of collective democratic agency to individual mobility, if you cannot solve the coordination problems abolition generates, if your alternative reproduces exclusion in a more pernicious interior form—then the intellectually honest conclusion is not "I retain the intuition but lack the institutional program." It is "the intuition may itself be defective, generated by an unexamined privileging of one set of interests over another, and unsupported by any workable account of political order." You have dismantled the superstructure and declared the foundation untouched. But the foundation was always the superstructure's product, not its source. The intuition that physical obstruction of movement across borders is uniquely gravely wrong was the conclusion of your framework, not its innocent starting point. You built the framework to vindicate the intuition, the framework collapsed, and now you are cradling the rubble and calling it bedrock.

I put it to you directly: you have not demonstrated that physical obstruction of civilian movement across borders is a grave act requiring extraordinary justification. You have asserted it, you have felt it, and you have failed every attempt to justify it. The appropriate response to this failure is not to preserve the intuition in formaldehyde as an unredeemed moral remainder. It is to examine whether a moral intuition that cannot be cashed out in any defensible institutional form, that depends on normative hierarchies you cannot supply, and that is held asymmetrically by those least affected by its consequences, is an intuition worth retaining at all.
